etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English expire, from Middle French expirer, from Latin exspīrō, exspīrāre, from ex- (“out”) + spīrō, spīrāre (“breathe, be alive”).

quote.citation: 1748, [Samuel Richardson], “Letter CXIII”, in Clarissa. Or, The History of a Young Lady: […], volume VII, London:  […]  S[amuel] Richardson;  […], →OCLC, page 415:
quote.text: And then, his head ſinking on his pillow, he expired; at about half an hour after ten.

quote.citation: 1764 December 24 (indicated as 1765), Onuphrio Muralto, translated by William Marshal [pseudonyms; Horace Walpole], chapter V, in The Castle of Otranto, […], London:  […]  Tho[mas] Lownds […], →OCLC, pages 190–191:
quote.text: Hippolita, ſcarce more alive than her daughter, was regardleſs of every thing but her: but when the tender Iſabella’s care would have likewiſe removed her, while the ſurgeons examined Matilda’s wound, ſhe cried, remove me! never! never! I lived but in her, and will expire with her.

quote.citation: 1833, R. J. Bertin, translated by Charles W. Chauncy, Treatise on the Diseases of the Heart, and Great Vessels, Philadelphia: Carey, Lea & Blnachard, page 185:
quote.text: Soon the patient had no longer sufficient strength to sit up; the trunk of the body was inclined to the right side, the head high and thrown backward, the mouth wide open: she seemed to stifle rather than respire: lastly, speech and respiration failed her; she uttered, however, in a feeble voice, some incoherent words, said she felt she was dying, and, accordingly, expired the sixth day after entrance.

quote.citation: 1961 November 10, Joseph Heller, “The Soldier in White”, in Catch-22 […], New York, N.Y.: Simon and Schuster, →OCLC, page 168:
quote.text: People bled to death like gentlemen in an operating room or expired without comment in an oxygen tent.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To come to an end; to conclude.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Revelation 20:7:
quote.text: And when the thousand yeeres are expired, Satan shall be loosed out of his prison,  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To exhale; to breathe out.

quote.citation: 1672, Gideon Harvey, Morbus Anglicus, Or, The Anatomy of Consumptions:
quote.text: Anatomy exhibits the lungs in a continual motion of inspiring and expiring air.
This chafed the boar; his nostrils flames expire.

quote.citation: 1843, Loring Dudley Chapin, (Please provide the book title or journal name):
quote.text: Animals expire carbon and plants inspire it; plants expire oxygen and animals inspire it.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To give forth insensibly or gently, as a fluid or vapour; to emit in minute particles.

quote.citation: 1627 (indicated as 1626), Francis [Bacon], “(please specify the page, or |century=I to X)”, in Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries. […], London:  […]  William Rawley […]; [p]rinted by J[ohn] H[aviland] for William Lee […], →OCLC:
quote.text: the expiring of cold out of the inward parts of the earth in winter

definitions.definition: (transitive) To bring to a close; to terminate.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1595 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Romeo and Ivliet”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iv]:
quote.text: Expire the term / Of a despised life.
